sections.title: The question this course answers
text: You're at vertex A. What is the smallest number of edges you must cross to reach every other vertex, and which vertices can't you reach at all? **Breadth-first search (BFS)** answers this.
By the end of the four modules you can do the five things in the table. Each module says which ones it covers.

rows: Describe a graph with the words vertex, edge and neighbour, and spot a vertex with no edges.
Read the neighbours of any vertex from a picture or a Python adjacency list.
Trace BFS with a queue, writing the queue down after every step.
Explain why a vertex is marked as found when it joins the queue, not when it leaves.
Find the route with the fewest edges, and name the vertices that can't be reached.

sections.title: How to use these pages
text: Each module is one page of numbered sections. Work top to bottom, or jump to a section with the **Learning guide**.
Press the speaker beside a section title to hear that section. The word being read turns green.
Every **Quick check** has a Show solution button. Try first, then look.
**Practice** gives you new questions for any module, as many times as you like. The **Full quiz** tests all the modules together, with 15 new questions every time.
**Settings** changes text size, font, spacing, colours, motion and captions. Use any of them, for any reason.

sections.title: Warm-up (no marks)
text: Six questions to see what you already know. Wrong answers are fine here: you get a one-line explanation, and the readiness report at the end of Module 4 compares your score with this one.

sections.title: Warm-up
sections.done_text: Thanks, that's your starting point. Module 2 starts with graphs.

questions.q: Draw each building on a map as a dot and each walkway as a line. What do you get?
questions.after: Dots joined by lines are a graph. Module 2 starts here.

questions.q: P, then Q, then R join a queue. Who is served first?
questions.after: A queue serves whoever joined first. BFS relies on that (Module 3).

questions.q: How many edges do you cross on the route A → C → E?
questions.after: Two edges: A–C and C–E. Count the lines, not the dots.

questions.q: An undirected edge joins B and D. Can you cross it from D to B?
Exploring outward from A, which do you visit first?
questions.after: Closer vertices come first: that's the idea behind BFS.

questions.q: F has no edges at all. Can you reach F from A?
questions.after: With no edges, nothing leads to F. Module 4 looks at this.
